# Codestrand

> Watch Git history take shape over time

---

Source: https://codestrand.pages.dev/

# Codestrand

![Codestrand logo](assets/codestrand.svg)

Watch a Git repository take shape over time. Files keep persistent positions while
contributors glide above the directory graph. Each commit connects a contributor to
all affected files; diff fragments show additions and removals.

![Codestrand playing Git histories in seven themes: repositories appear, grow and are archived, contributors send beams to changed files, and the camera flies in behind an avatar](assets/montage.webp)

Watch the [feature tour on YouTube](https://youtu.be/gmueXAHnvAE).

Codestrand has seven steady themes, labels, contributor
portraits and a mostly planar scene. Preview and export share a repeatable
simulation, including playback of multiple repositories. Export writes PNG frames or
streams video to your installed FFmpeg.

## Start here

1. [Install Codestrand](https://codestrand.pages.dev/getting-started/installation/).
2. [Play your repository](https://codestrand.pages.dev/getting-started/quickstart/).
3. Adjust [playback and camera controls](https://codestrand.pages.dev/playback/).
4. [Export frames](https://codestrand.pages.dev/export/) or set up [contributors and avatars](https://codestrand.pages.dev/contributors/).

Use [Git history import](https://codestrand.pages.dev/history/) for revisions and cache behaviour, and
[troubleshooting](https://codestrand.pages.dev/troubleshooting/) for platform and configuration problems.

## Acknowledgements

Codestrand is licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0. Thanks to
[Material Icon Theme](https://github.com/material-extensions/vscode-material-icon-theme)
for file icons (MIT), [Bevy](https://bevy.org/) for rendering,
[resvg](https://github.com/linebender/resvg) for SVG rasterisation,
[gix](https://github.com/GitoxideLabs/gitoxide) for Git access and
[Gource](https://gource.io/) for inspiration.

# Installation

Codestrand ships as a native binary. Choose a channel matching your tools.
The guides describe 0.2.0. Until publication, install from `main` for these features.
If an option in the guides is missing from `--help`, build from `main`:

```sh
cargo install --locked --git https://github.com/owenlamont/codestrand --branch main
```

This requires Rust and the native build prerequisites described below.
Check `codestrand --version` and the command's `--help` after installing.

## PyPI

With [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) and Python 3.11+:

```sh
uv tool install codestrand
```

## npm

With Node.js 18+:

```sh
npm install --global @owenlamont/codestrand
```

The wrapper selects a platform binary through optional dependencies. Keep optional
dependencies enabled when installing.

## crates.io

With [Rust](https://rustup.rs/) and the native build prerequisites:

```sh
cargo install --locked codestrand
```

Building from source compiles Bevy and can take several minutes. A checkout uses
Rust 1.99.1, pinned in `rust-toolchain.toml`.

## GitHub releases

Download a ZIP from [GitHub releases](https://github.com/owenlamont/codestrand/releases),
extract the archive and put `codestrand` (Windows: `codestrand.exe`) on your `PATH`.
Keep the included licences and third-party notices when redistributing the binary.
Compare the archive's SHA-256 digest with the release's `SHA256SUMS` file.

## Platforms

PyPI wheels, npm binaries and release ZIPs target:

- Linux with glibc 2.28+: x86-64 and ARM64.
- macOS: Apple Silicon (ARM64).
- Windows: x86-64 and ARM64.

There is no prebuilt Intel macOS or Linux musl binary. Rendering requires a working
graphics adapter; interactive preview also needs a windowing environment. History
inspection does not start the renderer. See [troubleshooting](https://codestrand.pages.dev/troubleshooting/)
for build and graphics problems.

## Verify

```sh
codestrand --version
codestrand --help
codestrand preview --help
```

Continue with [first use](https://codestrand.pages.dev/getting-started/quickstart/).

---

Source: https://codestrand.pages.dev/getting-started/quickstart/

# First use

## Play the current repository

```sh
codestrand preview
```

Run the command inside a Git working tree or one of its subdirectories. Codestrand
searches upward for the repository. Outside a repository, pass `--repository PATH`.
Escape closes the window.

## Play a local repository

```sh
codestrand preview --repository /path/to/repository
```

Replace the path with a local working or bare repository. Quote paths containing
spaces. Codestrand reads committed history without changing the repository;
uncommitted working-tree edits are not shown.

To choose a revision and a smaller playback window:

```sh
codestrand preview --repository /path/to/repository --revision HEAD \
  --start-date 2026-05-01 --end-date 2026-05-31
```

Both UTC date bounds are inclusive: playback includes the whole named end day.
Choose dates present in the repository. Omit either bound to use the beginning or
end of history; earlier commits are settled before playback.

## Next steps

- [Camera controls and pacing](https://codestrand.pages.dev/playback/).
- [Import and inspect history](https://codestrand.pages.dev/history/).
- [Export PNG frames](https://codestrand.pages.dev/export/).
- [Map contributor names and fetch portraits](https://codestrand.pages.dev/contributors/).

From a source checkout, replace `codestrand` with `cargo run --locked --`.
For smoother rendering, use `cargo run --locked --release --`.

---

Source: https://codestrand.pages.dev/history/

# Git history import

## Inspect a repository

```sh
codestrand inspect /path/to/repository --revision HEAD
```

Inspection reads a complete local working or bare repository without modifying
history. The experimental JSON lists the first-parent commits that change the tree,
oldest first, with raw author identities and paths and their file changes. Merge
changes compare against the first parent. Avoid treating the experimental schema as a
stable contract.

## Choose history for playback

```sh
codestrand preview --repository /path/to/repository --revision HEAD
```

Preview and export use the selected revision's first-parent timeline. Revision
defaults to `HEAD`. Codestrand does not clone or fetch a remote repository: obtain
a complete local repository first.

With `--start-date` or `--end-date`, import scans commit headers to find the range,
then reads one tree, the commit before the range, and the diffs inside the range.
Diffs before or after the range are not read, and import budgets apply to the range
read.

Revisions accept reference names, full or unambiguous abbreviated object IDs, and
`HEAD` (also `@`). Parent selectors `^N` and first-parent ancestor selectors `~N` can
be combined; `^{}` and `^{commit}` are accepted. Other Git revision expressions,
including reflog and message searches, are rejected rather than delegated to unbounded
reference traversal. Revision strings are limited to 4,096 bytes and navigation to
1,000,000 steps, with the existing object-size and work budgets applied before loading.
Annotated tags and symbolic references have a 64-hop limit and cycle detection.
Cyclic or excessive chains produce an error. Import reads no `.gitattributes`,
index or worktree, so `HEAD` matters only when it is the revision. Import uses no
wall-clock deadline.

## Analysis limits

Import refuses a history that exceeds a fixed safety limit, naming the budget and
the commit that exceeded it. Import reads the range newest first, so the refusal also
names a later `--start-date` whose range fits, or says that none does.

Blob size, diff input and per-diff comparison limits skip line detail only. Inspection
records the path, change kind and rename with diff kind `skipped`, without line counts
or samples. Playback retains the file event with zero line counts and no samples;
touch heat still applies. Skipped blobs still consume global work units. Once the
aggregate byte or line allowance is spent, older diffs also omit line detail.

| Budget | Limit |
| --- | --- |
| First-parent commits | 1,000,000 |
| Expanded entries per tree and retained changes overall | 2,000,000 each |
| Expanded path bytes per tree | 64 MiB |
| Tree depth and individual path bytes | 256 levels; 16,384 bytes |
| Single inflated object / allocation | 16 MiB |
| Inflated diff blob bytes overall | 8 GiB |
| Diff input lines overall | 20,000,000 |
| Potential line comparisons per diff | 1,000,000,000 |
| Total work charged for objects, bytes and lines | 32 GiB of work units |
| Accounted graph, tree and retained history storage | 512 MiB |

Tree summaries count repeated subtrees at every expanded location before diffing.
Object headers are checked before loading data; lines are counted before interning.
The storage budget accounts for payloads and overhead, rather than measuring process
RSS; dependency buffers and rendering need additional memory. Limits are fixed to keep
hostile inputs bounded; a later start reduces the history they are charged against.

## Cache

Repository playback saves the latest imported timeline, diff counts and bounded
line samples under the platform user cache directory, inside `codestrand/`.
Linked worktrees share a cache
namespace based on the canonical common Git directory. A different resolved tip,
start commit or end commit replaces the saved timeline after a complete import.
Changing pacing reuses the imported timeline. Contributor mapping edits take effect on
cache hits.

Cache errors regenerate data without blocking playback. To bypass history and
avatar cache reads and writes:

```sh
codestrand preview --repository /path/to/repository --no-cache
```

Inspection and repositories with Git replacement objects always import directly.
Messages, signatures, blob IDs and hunks are not cached. See
[contributors](https://codestrand.pages.dev/contributors/) for separately cached portraits.

Cache files are read only through real directories, with a 64 MiB byte ceiling before
JSON parsing. Version, selected tip, commit identifiers, event/change counts, paths,
author lengths, timestamps, diff counts and sample limits are checked before reuse.
Only the canonical snapshot encoding is accepted: padded, malformed or invalid snapshots
are misses and are rebuilt. Cache validation does not authenticate who wrote a snapshot.

---

Source: https://codestrand.pages.dev/playback/

# Playback

Preview loops the selected history. Export renders the same launch timeline at
explicit frame times, with a 1x playback multiplier and a fitted or scripted export camera.

Preview renders at the window's physical resolution, including on HiDPI displays.
Resizing or maximising keeps a 720-logical-pixel-high UI: text scales with height,
and wider windows show more scene. See [Export](https://codestrand.pages.dev/export/) for native output sizes.

Preview opens its window at once and shows planning progress until playback is ready.
For long histories, the first frame appears while later history is still being
planned. Playback pauses if planning falls behind, then resumes without skipping
history. Camera controls remain active during the pause, and a small label shows
the planning stage and percentage. Rewinding or looping may need another planning pause.
Export prints the stage and its percentage to standard error at most once a second.

Commit application times are planned ahead for the selected history and pacing.
The caption shows the last applied commit's date; cooling and fades advance in
playback seconds. Seeking or restarting replays the same fixed simulation ticks.
The caption's percentage follows history time, excluding extra walking waits, so it
holds while contributors finish a walk.

Repository captions also name the applying commit's repository, including single-tile
playback. The default
`--caption-style bar` tints the entire caption bar, matching the repository tile hue
and cross-fading for 0.3 playback
seconds, with at least 0.8 seconds between transitions (at least 0.5 seconds steady).
Rapid changes coalesce to the
latest repository when the hold expires; the caption text always updates immediately.
Both treatments use white text on opaque dark tints with at least 5.52:1 contrast.
`--caption-style chip` colours only the repository name's background instead.

Caption columns have fixed widths for the entire playback, including the lead-in.
Widths use the longest scheduled date, repository and resolved contributor name, plus
the total commit counter's digits. Speed and theme columns reserve their longest
available values so preview controls cannot move separators. Captions always use the
embedded monospace Fira Mono font, even when another theme uses proportional labels.
CLI playback uses the same six fixed columns for single and multiple repositories.

Text falls back from the selected theme font to bundled IBM Plex Mono for accented
and Cyrillic names, then to installed system fonts for other scripts, including Greek.
Install fonts covering the required scripts on export machines; use the same fonts when
comparing frames across machines.
Linux system-font discovery uses Fontconfig. Linux installations with no system fonts
are outside the supported configuration.
macOS discovers installed fonts through CoreText and Library/Fonts directories.

## Controls

| Input | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Escape | Release captured mouse; otherwise close preview |
| C | Capture or release the mouse while display settings are closed |
| Left click in viewport | Capture the mouse while display settings are closed |
| Mouse movement (captured) | Aim directly without holding a button |
| Hold left / right button (captured) | Move along world Y up / down; both cancel |
| F10 | Open or close display settings; release capture and pause camera controls |
| F11 | Toggle borderless fullscreen on the current monitor |
| `[` | Halve live speed, down to 0.125x |
| `]` | Double live speed, up to 8x |
| `,` / `.` | Previous or next theme |
| WASD | Move horizontally relative to yaw; release contributor follow |
| Right drag (released) | Orbit with world-Y yaw and pitch clamped to ±90° |
| Scroll wheel | Zoom; scroll the preset list when over display settings |
| Tab | Follow or cycle visible contributors |
| Space | Restore the fit-to-scene camera over half a second |

The caption shows the live multiplier, theme, camera mode and follow target. Following
returns to free camera when the target fades out. Preview controls do not change
the exported camera or timeline.

Preview starts with the cursor released. Capture hides and locks the cursor; C or
Escape releases capture, and another Escape closes preview. Opening F10 settings or
losing window focus also releases capture. Closing settings or returning to the window
does not recapture: press C or click the viewport again. Clicks in letterbox bars do
not capture. Capture and release discard that frame's mouse motion to avoid a jump.
Mouse aim uses 0.003 radians per mouse count, independent of frame time.
Held mouse buttons move at the WASD speed along world Y, independent of pitch.
Descending stops at floor clearance. The left click that
captures the mouse cannot move the camera until released and pressed again.

Display settings have a scrollable preset list with a draggable scrollbar. Monitor native
is first; other choices are grouped by aspect ratio, then ascending pixel size.
Ratios use conventional display names: 3440×1440 is labelled 21:9.

| Aspect | Presets (physical pixels) |
| --- | --- |
| 16:9 | 1280×720, 1600×900, 1920×1080, 2560×1440, 3840×2160 |
| 16:10 | 1280×800, 1920×1200, 2560×1600 |
| 21:9 | 2560×1080, 3440×1440, 3840×1600 |
| 32:9 | 3840×1080, 5120×1440 |

Choices exceeding either dimension of the current monitor are greyed out with a reason
and cannot be selected. Windowed choices resize the window after restoring normal
window placement; the desktop may further constrain the actual window size.

In borderless fullscreen, presets keep fullscreen and render at exactly the selected
pixel size, centred with black bars around the unused monitor area. No preset is
upscaled. Monitor native fills the display. Captions and other UI stay inside the
rendered viewport, scaled by its height rather than the full monitor height.
F11 restores the previous windowed size and position. Playback continues while
settings are open; mouse wheel input over the panel scrolls instead of zooming.

The default camera looks straight down at the centre of the repository tile area.
Repository tiles are rectangles in world coordinates. Preview stores yaw and pitch
explicitly, with no roll. Yaw rotates about world Y; pitch rotates about the camera's
local right axis and clamps to −90° through +90°, inclusive. The camera can look
exactly straight down or up, and yaw still rotates the view at either pole.
Camera up never opposes world up. The eye stays at least 1.2 world units above the plane,
above the glass and file geometry, and can look up at contributors at height 3.2.
Vertical mouse motion changes pitch; horizontal motion changes yaw. Captured mouse
aim turns about the eye in free mode. WASD uses forward and right from yaw alone,
stays horizontal and remains well-defined when looking straight down or up.
Right-drag orbit remains available with the cursor released.
Orbit, captured aim and zoom retain the followed
contributor as the aim; WASD or button elevation releases follow. Released right-drag
and follow orbit use the same yaw and pitch limits. At the floor, free orbit turns about
the eye instead of crossing the plane; zoom slides along the floor.
Follow shortens its orbit radius at the floor while keeping its aim on the contributor.
Space smoothly raises the eye and restores the
overhead view with yaw 0°, pitch −90° and camera up pointing toward −Z.

Export defaults to the overhead perspective camera at explicit frame times;
[scripted paths](https://codestrand.pages.dev/export/#scripted-camera) can override the view. Default
framing reserves space for elevated avatars and labels; clearance guarantees apply to
the fitted view. Free orbit and zoom can crop content. File glyphs lie flat with upright
artwork in the overhead view. Directory structures, membership rings and activity halos
remain on the file plane.
Avatar portraits face the camera.
The plane cannot be viewed from underneath; glass and file surfaces use backface culling.

## Themes

`--theme` selects the starting theme for preview and export;
the default is `neon`. Switching themes in preview changes styling:
layout, playback position and camera stay put.

The seven themes are `neon`, `phosphor`, `outrun`, `blueprint`,
`retro-desktop`, `atlas` and `forge`. Choose one for preview or export:

```sh
codestrand preview --theme outrun
codestrand export frames --theme atlas --frames 90 --fps 30
```

Every theme shows each file's type icon. Outrun frames icons in pink tiles and uses
arched beams and a banded sunset. Blueprint frames them in outlined plates and uses
construction lines. Retro Desktop draws them on pages and uses static black/white
dashed beams. Atlas uses paper contours and tinted top-level territories. Forge cuts
icons through iron plates coloured by file heat.
Blueprint and Atlas use ink without additive glow. All grounds and dash patterns
are steady; switching with `,` and `.` preserves playback and file positions.

## File heat

Each non-deletion touch adds heat based on added plus removed lines. Logarithmic
damping keeps large changes from overwhelming small ones; repeated touches
accumulate up to a cap.
Neon and Phosphor brighten file icons through 32 shared brightness levels while
cold icons remain readable. Heat below 0.001 settles to zero. Activity halos pulse
on every touch and decay independently with a 1.6-second time constant, unaffected
by diff size or the heat half-life.

Forge maps the same 32 heat buckets from dark iron through red and orange to
white heat. Only warm plates contribute to thresholded bloom. Blueprint, Atlas
and Retro Desktop keep constant ink brightness; touched files still receive
activity outlines.

`--heat-half-life 3` sets the cooling half-life in canonical playback seconds for
preview and export (default `3`, accepted range `0.01` through `86400`, inclusive).
Live speed keys speed up cooling along with the rest of playback. Export cooling uses
explicit frame times. Files settled before the inclusive start date begin cold.

```sh
codestrand export frames --heat-half-life 3 --frames 90 --fps 30
```

## Multiple repositories

Repeat `--repository` to play local repositories on one author-time timeline:

```sh
codestrand preview --repository /path/to/first --repository /path/to/second
```

Alternatively, pass `--repositories-file repositories.toml` to preview or export:

```toml
[[repositories]]
path = "/path/to/first"
label = "First project"
archived = true

[[repositories]]
path = "../second"
ended = "2026-05-01"
```

Paths in the TOML file resolve relative to the file. Labels default to the repository
directory name. Repeated flags and a file can be combined; flag entries come first.
Paths resolving to the same location are rejected as duplicate repositories. Labels for
distinct repositories must be unique. There is no fixed repository-count limit.
When minimum tiles and gutters cannot fit the field, tiles, gutters, avatars and titles
shrink by one detail scale chosen before playback, as if the camera pulled back.
Tile packing time grows steeply with repository count.

`archived = true` ends a repository after the final commit in the selected revision,
once the commit's activity finishes. `ended = "YYYY-MM-DD"` supplies an explicit UTC
ending date and overrides `archived`, for example after deletion. The repository is
shown through the end of that day, inclusive: `ended = "2026-05-01"` includes all of
1 May UTC and begins ending at 00:00 UTC on 2 May. A commit after the ending in
imported history order is an error, even when a rebased commit has an older author
date. The error names the first offending commit and a valid ending date.
Neither field fetches platform metadata. Without either field the repository remains
visible.
An ending before the selected playback interval is already complete when playback starts.

The ending tile, files and directories grey, rise and fade over 2.5 playback seconds.
Neighbours then reclaim the space over four seconds. Text fades in place.

## Contributor and file lifecycles

The first commit enlarges the contributor avatar, settling over 1.2 playback seconds.
Whole-file additions descend from the contributor along the beam to the file layout;
deletions grey, rise and fade over 1.2 seconds. Line fragments remain separate.

`--contributor-inactivity-days 60` assumes a contributor has left after 60 calendar
days without a commit across the combined history. The avatar greys and fades over
1.2 playback seconds; another commit revives the same contributor. The two-month default
flags Owen's observed 88-day pause in the combined first-parent histories.
Departure is an assumption, not platform knowledge. Deadlines follow the compressed,
padded timeline, using the latest author date reached so reversed dates cannot trigger
an immediate departure. Playback does not extrapolate contributor departures beyond
the final history date.

```sh
codestrand preview --repositories-file repositories.toml \
  --contributor-inactivity-days 60
```

Repository manifests must be regular files no larger than 1 MiB.
Repository paths are limited to 4,096 bytes before filesystem resolution.

Events merge by comparing the next commit from each repository by author timestamp,
breaking ties by repository input order. Each repository retains its first-parent
order, including children authored before their parents. One `--revision` applies
to every repository; `--start-date` and `--end-date`
select from the merged history. Single-repository playback retains first-parent
order. Contributor mappings apply across all repositories, so a matched contributor
uses one avatar that moves between regions.

Live repositories share the inset viewport inside a 24-pixel frame margin. The
same frame-scaled avatar sizing and gutter placement apply to single repositories.
The top wordmark has a separate 26-pixel reserved strip, including
a four-pixel buffer;
avatars, gutter routes and name labels stay below the strip, matching caption clearance.
The default 16:9 export camera stays fixed. Spacing and size floors use a fixed world scale
calibrated in reference pixels; apparent ground spacing is slightly smaller to reserve
room for elevated portraits. Preview orbit changes the projection, not the packing.
Shared gutters separate neighbouring tiles, with no
contributor band. Tile weights follow eased square roots of live file counts;
empty active repositories retain weight one. Each repository keeps file identity,
local layout and one uniform scale, with a fixed quarter-turn chosen for its history.
Content zoom anticipates growth with a precomputed safe-fit envelope and half-second
easing. The log-scale limit is 0.12 per second when zooming out and 0.08 when zooming in
(about 11.3% shrink or 8.3% growth). A larger future contraction can start the
adjustment earlier; the chosen scale never exceeds the tile's current safe fit.
The usable content area leaves an eight-pixel edge inset. Corner titles share one
character size, which shrinks once each repository's share of the field holds fewer
than four minimum tiles, reaching about half size at 72 repositories and never below
6 pixels. They end in an ellipsis when wider than their tile and sit 4 pixels from the
tile edge, instead of one avatar diameter, on tiles too small for that clearance; they
are omitted only from tiles too short for the text.
Directory and touched-file labels shrink with their tile's files, are never larger than
the corner titles, stop at the same 6 pixel floor, and end in an ellipsis when wider than
their tile. Invisible archived
content cannot constrain earlier zoom.

A newcomer splits one existing tile or subtree. Other repositories retain their
relative order. Splits clamp to a ground-aspect range of 1:2.5 to 2.5:1, inclusive,
and a 144-by-64 reference-pixel floor at full detail. Births ease for up to 0.75
playback seconds before their first commit; births near the lead-in use the available
lead-in time. Aspect and size clamps scale with presence during the transition.
Tiles and shared gutters partition the whole inset field. `--gutter` sets the visible
spacing in 1280×720 reference pixels: default `4`, range `0`–`20`, inclusive,
including touching tiles at `0`. Crowd scaling shrinks avatars and names when many are
active.
Names prefer clear content rectangles, including repository labels
and a small margin, but may overlap content near tile edges when space is tight.
Different content shapes can leave space inside a uniformly fitted tile.

Contributor names orbit at no more than 30 degrees per playback second, with a
three-second minimum between direction reversals. A new position must reduce the
currently occluded text area by at least a quarter for 0.75 playback seconds before
the name moves. Brief overlap is preferable to fast or oscillating text.

Close zoom keeps inactive file and directory names visible. Names appear when the
smaller dimension of the object's projected footprint reaches 48 logical pixels and
remain until the footprint drops below 40 pixels. These names bypass the activity and
landmark limits. Names use fixed world anchors and upright text; long names can overlap.
The same rules apply to preview and export, using each mode's camera.

Contributors first appear in a gutter slot above their repository, aligned with the
projected mean of touched files. Switching repositories chooses the nearest valid edge
instead of requiring a detour to the top. A slot survives consecutive commits while
its beam and frame checks remain valid.
Placement checks the touched files throughout service, including
additions and deletions, for an open half-plane and beams crossing another repository
or its label.
Other edges provide fallback docks. Avatars spread along edges; names shrink to a readable
minimum, then move to free nearby lanes before truncating as a last resort. Names remain
visible with their avatars. Portrait size accounts for perspective.

Avatar travel follows gutter centrelines and the outer margin. Parking slots
sit on the same network. Routes never cross tile interiors, including unused areas;
portraits may overlap tile edges beside a narrow gutter. Dijkstra minimises network
length. Other avatars have no travel cost: walkers never wait or detour for each other.
Parking still spreads avatars when clear slots are available.

A contributor can depart once its previous commit's last fragment has arrived and the
moving gutter route can meet the speed limit. Travel overlaps other contributors'
animations; commits remain strictly chronological. Routes stop at corners and accelerate
toward `--avatar-max-speed` reference pixels/second (default `480`, minimum `1`).
Moving junctions follow the gutter network, with every canonical sample checked against
the speed limit, frame bounds and tile guards. A shared parking point creates no trip.
Contributors follow their parked gutter slot until their inferred calendar departure,
then fade over 1.2 playback seconds. Capped playback releases faded lanes and re-enters
at the next service slot after a long idle gap.

`--contributor-travel auto` is the default: contributors walk short trips and fade
when a longer route would delay the commit. `--contributor-travel walk` keeps them
walking along the shortest safe gutter route, waiting as long as needed.
`--bot-travel fade` is the default for bots; `--bot-travel walk` gives bots the same
travel policy selected for other contributors. Bot classification uses an explicit
`bot` override
in `contributors.toml`, then a GitHub noreply login ending in `[bot]`, then the displayed
name's `[bot]` suffix. Travel policies also apply to single repositories.
Walking avatars remain visible during travel until an inferred calendar departure.
With `--contributor-travel walk`, walking trips
also remain routed across long idle gaps instead of disappearing and re-entering at a
different repository. After the last service, the normal inactivity fade still applies.
Uncapped walking services trips in commit order and adds another second of waiting
when tile motion or insufficient travel time blocks a route. New repository tiles get
a full 0.75-second birth window inside their added wait. At the start of a wait,
tile sizes transition toward the upcoming commit for at most 0.75 seconds,
finishing before arrival. Tiles then hold their size, using the upcoming commit's
zoom ceiling while fitting the content from before the commit. The content outline
switches on arrival without moving the tile. Layout and calendar departures follow
history time, which holds during travel waits. An uncapped plan
that cannot find safe routes within the planning budgets reports an error instead of
silently accepting a travel fade.
A plan that cannot converge within 32 replans stops with an error.
Dormant contributors follow their previous repository's lane while waiting, so later
tile growth cannot bury the starting point of their next uncapped trip.
The caption holds the last applied date during waiting; heat, fragments and fades
continue in presentation seconds.

```sh
codestrand export frames --repositories-file repositories.toml \
  --contributor-travel walk --bot-travel walk --avatar-max-speed 480 --frames 90 --fps 30
```

Planning tests departure ticks from the contributor's fragment completion onward.
Gaps between that contributor's commits absorb travel before padding is needed.
Padding is revalidated as scene geometry changes. The automatic policy uses at most five
padded rebuilds, including one cleanup of unused service padding.
Uncapped padding grows until every walking trip completes, subject to the planning
memory estimate. Each Dijkstra search is limited to 10,000 graph nodes.
Numeric caps apply to accumulated extra waiting per commit.

Header and caption remain in the outer frame. Other preview aspect ratios use conservative
framing;
free-camera controls remain independent.

Planning snapshots the machine's available physical memory before importing history.
Swap does not count. An estimate above that snapshot is refused, with both values
reported in bytes and MiB. If memory information cannot be read, planning stops.
The estimate uses the actual selected schedule, repository samples, contributor
first arrivals, imported changes, path bytes and directory samples. Variable allocation
sizes are estimates, so the figure is not a process-memory ceiling. Each padded schedule
is checked before rebuilding; the automatic policy does not reserve hypothetical waits.
The same check applies to single repositories.

Use fewer repositories or a later inclusive `--start-date` to reduce the estimate.
The snapshot is not a memory reservation; other processes can consume RAM afterward.
It is the host's available RAM, without container or job-specific memory limits.
Rendering and video encoding need additional memory beyond the planning estimate.
The check is an estimate made before planning, not a guarantee that the process will
fit in memory. It can be conservative on some inputs and too low on others.
Packing reserves tiles before applying repository endings, so sequential repositories
share the detail scale of repositories visible together.
Route searches stop at 10,000 nodes; capped playback can fade across when a search
exceeds that bound, while uncapped walking reports an error.

Large multi-repository histories can take time to begin playback. Consumed travel plans
are discarded to bound retained travel windows and checkpoints; the shared layout
remains available throughout playback. This does not bound total process memory.
To inspect a smaller interval, use inclusive `--start-date` and `--end-date`.

Playback memory and duration checks use the range selected by `--start-date` and `--end-date`;
the layout estimate also includes the files present when the range starts.

To choose visual treatments, use
`--repository-boundary none|glass` and `--repository-label-plane files|raised`.
Defaults are `glass` and `raised`. Glass is a faint, coloured ground-plane tile for
each live repository; raised labels stay at a constant height of 1.6 scene units.
Both options apply to preview and export, including single repositories.

## Range and pacing

Import refuses a history over budget before planning or rendering. The error names
the exhausted budget, the commit and its UTC author date, and a later `--start-date`
whose range fits, or says that none does.

Import budgets are 1,000,000 commits, 2,000,000 changed entries, 20,000,000 diff input
lines and 512 MiB of retained-input accounting per repository.

Single-object and single-tree limits stay fixed, including 16 MiB objects, 2,000,000
expanded tree entries, depth 256, 16,384-byte paths and 64 MiB of expanded path bytes.
The 32 GiB cumulative work ceiling, 8 GiB blob-detail budget and per-diff work limits
also stay fixed. Oversized or expensive blob diffs keep file changes but omit detail;
exhausting the cumulative line budget also omits detail. Date bounds reduce import
work: diffs outside the range are not read. The caption still numbers commits
against the whole first-parent history.

```sh
codestrand preview --repository /path/to/repository --start-date 2026-05-01 --end-date 2026-05-31 \
  --seconds-per-day 2 --max-idle-seconds 1
```

- `--start-date YYYY-MM-DD`: first commit in merged order authored on or after
  00:00 UTC that day, inclusive; playback opens on the tree of the commit before it.
- `--end-date YYYY-MM-DD`: last commit in merged order authored on or before that
  UTC day, inclusive of the whole day. Omitted bounds use the beginning or end of
  history. A reversed range or one containing no commits reports both bounds.

Selection is a contiguous span of merged history. Rebased commits with older author
dates remain in that span; date bounds do not reorder or remove interior commits.

- `--seconds-per-day`: timeline seconds per calendar day; default `0.5`.
- `--max-idle-seconds`: maximum timeline gap between commits; default `1`.

```sh
codestrand preview --repository /path/to/repository --start-date 2026-05-01 --end-date 2026-05-31
```

Pacing preserves within-day timestamp spacing. Coincident, reversed or very close
timestamps get a 0.05-second minimum gap, limited by the idle cap, preserving commit
order. Seconds per day accepts `0.01` through `86400`, inclusive; the idle cap must
also be at least one simulation tick (1/60 second).

Live speed keys move through the canonical timeline faster or slower without
changing commit times, layout, pulses, beams, avatar motion, settling or fades in
timeline seconds. Changing live speed preserves the current position.

Commits affecting more than 24 files aim beams at directories to reduce clutter.

## Overview detail

Directory collapsing is on by default. Use `--collapse-directories off` in preview
or export to keep every file and directory visible at every zoom. Drawing every file
can reduce frame rate in large repositories. `--collapse-directories on` restores
aggregation. The option affects rendering only; file identity, layout and playback
remain unchanged.

Small subtrees containing multiple files collapse into folder glyphs below a 32-pixel screen
footprint. Zooming in expands the subtree above 40 pixels; the gap prevents
flicker near the boundary. Each touch expands the affected subtree and
its ancestors for 2.5 playback seconds, independently of heat. Files and folders scale
between the two views over 0.3 real seconds in preview and 0.3 playback seconds in export.
Footprints use logical pixels and a bounding circle to stay stable during orbit.

Collapsed folders have the theme's file-glyph footprint at the directory's scale,
centred on the directory and raised clear of file surfaces. Folders shrink with the
repository instead of growing to a minimum screen size.

Aggregation changes rendering only. Every directory and file keeps the same
simulation and position at every zoom, including export. Directory landmarks rank by
subtree size, with at most four extra top-level labels beyond the usual twenty.
Labels inside fully collapsed subtrees and overlapping directory labels are omitted
to keep the overview readable.

In repository playback, sampled added lines descend from the contributor; removed
lines rise from the file and smoothly fade to transparent. The camera-facing snippet
is the fragment, following the same path and phase above beams, with
a text shadow and theme backing for contrast. Text and plain prisms crossfade; fully
visible snippets replace their prisms. Extra fragments stay plain. Every theme supplies
added/removed colours; Atlas uses dark ink on its light ground. Snippets use alpha
blending and the theme's monospace font, with IBM Plex Mono for Atlas code beside its
serif labels.
Theme switching restyles active snippets without restarting their motion or fade.

`--fragment-speed` scales how fast fragments cross their beams in preview and export
(default `1`, about 0.9 playback seconds per crossing; accepted range `0.25` through
`2`, inclusive). `0.5` doubles the crossing time, giving snippets longer to read.
A walking contributor stays until its last fragment lands before leaving for its
next repository, and a slower setting also delays a calendar departure until then.
Commits keep their timeline spacing unless a walking trip needs the extra wait;
`--contributor-travel auto` may still fade a contributor across mid-flight.

```sh
codestrand export frames --fragment-speed 0.5 --frames 90 --fps 30
```

Snippet text keeps the font's natural proportions with equal X and Y scaling.
Lines are cut at 88 characters. Samples are hidden at 6 projected beam-diameter
pixels or less and fully visible at 14 or more, with a smooth transition between.
Visible text stays between 14 and 20 logical pixels high, inclusive, making close
oblique shots readable while the overview keeps plain fragments.
Text holds full contrast through the first three quarters of the fragment's alpha
fade, then fades out with the backing.
Overlapping snippets may overlap freely without collision or viewport-edge hiding.
Files inside collapsed subtrees show no sample text; LOD keeps its fragment behaviour.

Samples come from actual changed lines: up to three per file and twelve per commit,
preferring lines of 16–60 bytes, inclusive. Lines over 72 bytes before trimming,
non-ASCII text, controls and trivial lines are omitted. Binary files and submodules
have no samples.
Selection is deterministic; crowded commits use path order to spend the budget.
At most twelve samples appear at once.

**Source lines can contain secrets or personal information.** Review exports before
sharing. Sensitive paths (`.env*`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `id_rsa*`) and common credential
patterns are skipped, but filtering cannot guarantee redaction. Use
`--no-diff-samples` for preview or export to hide all sampled source lines. The
opt-out controls playback; bounded samples may still exist in the history cache.

The history cache stores these bounded samples. Older cache versions are rebuilt
automatically from local Git history.

---

Source: https://codestrand.pages.dev/export/

# Export

## Numbered PNG frames

```sh
codestrand export frames --repository /path/to/repository --start-date 2026-05-01 --end-date 2026-05-31
```

The output directory (`frames` here) must not already exist. Without a repository
argument or manifest, export discovers the repository from the current directory,
searching upward. Export writes `frame-00000.png` onwards and a
`frames.csv` logical-state manifest. Frames default to 1280×720.
The final `glyphs` and `missing_glyphs` columns count visible text-layout glyphs
used for each captured frame. A nonzero missing count indicates unavailable glyphs;
install fonts covering the contributor names' scripts before exporting again.

Select a native render size with `--resolution WIDTHxHEIGHT`:

```sh
codestrand export hd-frames --resolution 1920x1080 --frames 2
codestrand export uhd-frames --resolution 3840x2160 --frames 2
```

Each side accepts 64–8192 pixels, inclusive, with at most 33,554,432 pixels per frame
(including 7680×4320). The graphics adapter must support the selected texture size
and have enough memory. Both PNG and video exports render at the selected size
from the start. No upscaling is used. The default H.264 encoder needs even dimensions;
use PNGs or a suitable custom encoder for odd dimensions.

Export and preview share a 720-logical-pixel-high UI. Text, captions, labels and
diff snippets scale with frame height; wider aspect ratios reveal more scene
without stretching it. Preview renders at the window's physical resolution,
including after resize, maximise or fullscreen and with display scaling enabled.
Display scaling does not multiply the height-based text size a second time.

By default the whole playback is exported at 30 fps. To make a short capture:

```sh
codestrand export short-frames --frames 60 --fps 30
```

`--frames` accepts 2 through 4,294,967,295, inclusive, matching the supported frame
index range; `--fps` accepts 1 through 240, inclusive. An explicit
frame count stops capture after that many frames rather than changing the timeline
speed.

Export accepts the same repository, revision, range, pacing, contributor and cache
options as preview. By default, the camera uses the fit-to-scene view. Explicit frame
times keep export independent of rendering speed. Each capture is confirmed
written before export completes. Export needs a working graphics adapter.

## Progress

Export prints one line to stderr every 10 seconds:

```text
Exported 4510 frames; history 100.6/153.5s (65.6%); video 2:30 of ~6:09 (~11091 frames); 0:50 elapsed, ETA ~1:12
```

The percentage is history rendered so far. Until planning reaches the end of history,
`~` marks a projected video length and ETA: the waits planned so far, scaled to every
commit.
Waits grow as more contributors arrive, so the projection and ETA usually rise later.
When rendering has waited 10 seconds or more for planning, export prints a `Waiting for
planning` line with how long it has waited.
Set `RUST_LOG=info` to see graphics adapter details.

Diff snippets appear in close views, including scripted camera paths. Their text stays
14–20 logical pixels high (inclusive); the twelve-sample limit and collapsed-directory
hiding still apply. Snippets may overlap.

Moving translucent surfaces overlap using their current positions. Halos and glyphs
can look different from older builds.

Repeated PNG exports produce byte-identical frames and `frames.csv` manifests on the
same machine, graphics driver and build, with the same graphics backend, repository
history, options and portrait assets. Overlapping solid shapes of different colours
keep a stable draw order.
Use cached or local portraits offline: leave `--fetch-avatars` off and keep the avatar
cache unchanged between exports. Live fetching can change portraits with network
availability, deadlines and cache expiry. Fetch portraits before making repeatable captures.

## Stream a video to FFmpeg

```sh
codestrand export clip-state --video history.mp4 --frames 60 --fps 30
```

`--video` streams RGB frames directly to your installed FFmpeg instead of writing
PNGs. The required new directory (`clip-state`) still receives `frames.csv`.
The video path is relative to the current working directory. Choose a new video
filename; existing videos are refused. Codestrand never downloads, bundles or
links an encoder.

FFmpeg is found on PATH. `CODESTRAND_FFMPEG` selects another executable;
`--ffmpeg /path/to/ffmpeg` takes precedence. Paths containing spaces are supported
when quoted. Install FFmpeg with `winget install Gyan.FFmpeg` on Windows,
`brew install ffmpeg` on macOS, or your distribution's `ffmpeg` package on Linux.
PNG export works without FFmpeg.

The default encode uses `-c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -crf 18 -movflags +faststart`
for an H.264 MP4 suitable for GitHub, X, Bluesky and QuickTime. Before planning,
Codestrand runs FFmpeg and encodes one blank frame at the chosen resolution with the
default options; custom options are not tried until the export. Install a
libx264-enabled build if the default encoder is unavailable, or replace the encoding
options:

```sh
codestrand export lossless-state --video history.mkv --frames 60 \
  --ffmpeg-arg=-c:v --ffmpeg-arg=ffv1
```

Repeat `--ffmpeg-arg=VALUE` for every argument, including option values. Supplying
any arguments replaces **all** default encoding options. Arguments are passed
directly without shell expansion, after the fixed raw RGB input and before the
video filename. Select codecs, filters, pixel format and container options there;
input dimensions and frame rate come from Codestrand. Frame times stay explicit,
independent of encoding speed. Stderr is drained concurrently, and failures
include FFmpeg's diagnostic tail. Frame writes have a 30-second timeout. After the
last frame, Codestrand waits while the output file's size or modification time
changes; 30 seconds without either changing fails the export. Finalizing a large
video can therefore take longer than 30 seconds. Failed exports may leave a
partial video and manifest.

## Encode PNG frames manually

With external
[FFmpeg](https://github.com/FFmpeg/FFmpeg) and its libx264 encoder, encode a 30 fps
sequence:

```sh
ffmpeg -framerate 30 -i frames/frame-%05d.png -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p history.mp4
```

Match `-framerate` to the `--fps` used for export. Choose a new output filename;
FFmpeg asks before replacing an existing file. Keep PNGs for re-encoding or remove
them manually after checking the video.

## Scripted camera

`--camera-path` replaces the fitted export camera with TOML keys. Save the
[example path](examples/camera-path.toml) as `camera-path.toml` in a Git working
tree, then run there:

```sh
codestrand export camera-frames --camera-path camera-path.toml \
  --frames 241 --fps 30 --video camera.mkv --ffmpeg-arg=-c:v --ffmpeg-arg=ffv1
```

The file must be a regular file of at most 1 MiB. It requires `fps` (1–240, inclusive)
and one or more `[[key]]` tables. Each key requires an unsigned `frame`, `eye` and
`focus`. Frames must increase strictly. Key seconds are `frame / file fps`; export
`--fps` samples the same path at its own rate.
A path never changes playback speed or export duration. Frame zero follows the
selected inclusive start date; before the first key and after the last, the endpoint key
continues resolving its targets.

```toml
fps = 30
[[key]]
frame = 30
eye = { point = [0.0, 24.0, 16.0] }
focus = { point = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] }
[[key]]
frame = 60
eye = { avatar = "Ada", offset = [0.0, 6.0, 8.0] }
focus = { avatar = "Ada" }
```

Each anchor selects exactly one of `point`, `avatar`, `file` or `directory`.
Coordinates and optional `offset` vectors use world units: +Y is up, with files
on the XZ plane. Offsets remain world-aligned. Contributor names match resolved
display names exactly; ambiguous names fail.
File and directory paths match repository-relative layout strings, including case.
An empty directory path selects the repository root. A `repository`
label can qualify a file or directory; without the label, an ambiguous path reports
candidate repositories. Paths are matched, never opened by the camera evaluator.

Targets resolve from the simulation's current world positions on every frame,
including arrival/deletion effects. Avatars retain their simulation positions after
leaving, but have none before first creation. A referenced target without a position
fails with the output frame, key and target name; there is no origin fallback.
The first key must use points or targets already present at playback start. Hold a point
view until a target exists before blending toward that target's key.

A file target follows the same file through renames. A name used by multiple file
identities is ambiguous; choose another historical name. Re-adding after a deletion's
fade completes creates a new identity, so pacing can affect ambiguity.
Directories bind directly to the loaded layout, including planned positions before
appearance and outside the selected playback interval. There is no follow
filter: target motion retains the simulation's fixed 60 Hz ticks, which can show
steps at high output rates. Smoothstep blends the two keys' current eye/focus
positions; a repeated target follows throughout the segment without easing to a stop.

`up` inherits from the preceding key and defaults to `[0, 0, -1]`, suitable for
straight-down views. Normalised up vectors blend with smoothstep; orientation is
constructed from the resolved eye, focus and up, without Euler interpolation.
Opposite consecutive ups fail. Unknown fields, non-finite coordinates, invalid
ordering and unknown targets fail before the GPU, encoder or output directory starts.
Each output frame also rejects an eye below the 1.2-unit camera floor, coincident
eye/focus, or up parallel to the view. A later invalid pose can leave partial output.
Right/forward turns >90°/frame fail; add a key, raise fps, or lengthen the move.

The same inputs, including fps, produce the same logical camera poses regardless
of render delays. Rendered pixels can differ across graphics adapters, backends and
drivers, and slightly between runs. Camera paths affect export only; preview controls
remain independent.
Close-zoom names still enter at 48 pixels and leave below 40 pixels during camera moves.

---

Source: https://codestrand.pages.dev/configuration/

# Config file

`--config FILE` reads `preview` and `export` options from a TOML file, so a run can be
kept and repeated as one file. Each key is a flag name without the leading dashes:

```toml
seconds-per-day = 2
start-date = "2025-01-01"
gutter = 8
caption-style = "chip"
no-diff-samples = true
fps = 60
video = "history.mp4"

[[repositories]]
path = "../first"
label = "First project"

[[repositories]]
path = "../second"
```

```sh
codestrand preview --config codestrand.toml
codestrand export frames --config codestrand.toml --start-date 2025-06-01
```

- Flags on the command line override the file. A repeated flag such as `--repository`
  replaces the file's list rather than adding to it, and any `--repository` or
  `--repositories-file` flag replaces the whole repository list, and the file's list
  is then not read.
- One file serves both commands: an export option such as `fps` is checked but ignored
  by `preview`.
- Relative paths resolve beside the file, as repository paths do. `ffmpeg` is the
  exception, because a bare name is looked up on `PATH`.
- Switches such as `no-cache` take `true` or `false`. A switch set to `true` in the file
  cannot be turned off from the command line.
- Repeatable flags take a list, such as `repository = ["../first", "../second"]`.
- The `[[repositories]]` tables use the
  [repositories file](https://codestrand.pages.dev/playback/#multiple-repositories) format. A file holding them
  cannot also set `repositories-file`.
- Unknown keys and invalid values are errors that name the key.
- The export directory is a positional argument and stays on the command line.

Codestrand reads a config file only when `--config` names it. A file can enable avatar
fetching or choose the FFmpeg executable, so treat one from elsewhere like a script.

---

Source: https://codestrand.pages.dev/contributors/

# Contributors and avatars

Preview and export read `contributors.toml` from the user configuration directory:

- Linux: `~/.config/codestrand/` (or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/codestrand/` when set).
- macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/codestrand/`.
- Windows: `%APPDATA%\codestrand\`.

Override the file with `--contributors /path/to/contributors.toml`:

```toml
[[contributor]]
name = "Owen Lamont"
emails = ["owen@personal.example", "owen@work.example"]
github = "owenlamont"           # optional GitHub login
gitlab = "owenlamont"           # optional GitLab.com username
gravatar = "owen@avatar.example" # optional Gravatar email
bot = false                   # optional bot classification override
# avatar = "portraits/owen.png"  # optional local path or HTTPS URL; overrides lookups
```

Emails match case-insensitively; duplicate emails are errors. Matching names never merge
people with different nonempty emails. Unlisted emails keep separate identities,
displayed with the name from the last commit in playback order. Commits without an email
are grouped by author name. A missing default file is fine; an explicit missing file,
unknown key or malformed TOML is an error. Edits take effect on cache hits; original
authors and repository history remain unchanged.

`bot = true` marks automation and `bot = false` marks a human, overriding automatic
detection even after a display-name change. Without an override, a parsed GitHub noreply
login ending in `[bot]` identifies a bot; a displayed name ending in `[bot]` is the
fallback. `[bot]` elsewhere in a name does not match. Bot avatars fade between
repositories by default; use `--bot-travel walk` to route them like humans.

Configuration is limited to 1 MiB before parsing, 4,096 contributors, 4,096 total email
aliases, and 4,096 bytes per string. Expanded alias payloads may total at most 16 MiB.
Files exceeding a limit are rejected with a configuration error before alias expansion.

Account fields accept usernames, never profile URLs or whitespace. GitHub logins use
letters, digits and hyphens (bot logins may end in `[bot]`); GitLab usernames start with
a letter or digit and may also contain `_`, `-` and `.`. Invalid fields report the file,
contributor and field. Local avatar paths resolve relative to the TOML file and must stay
inside the TOML file's directory. Absolute paths are accepted only inside that directory.
Parent escapes, symlinks, directory junctions, network paths and device paths are rejected
before opening an image. Rejected paths warn and use the default coloured sphere.
All ancestors must be real directories, including ancestors of the TOML directory.
Local images
must decode as PNG, JPEG or GIF, at most 4 MiB and 2048 pixels per side. Missing or
undecodable local images produce a warning and fall back to account lookups.
Remote overrides require an HTTPS URL without credentials.

## Contributor avatars

Contributors stay above the file plane and move between repository service lanes.
`--avatar-scale` controls disc diameter relative to the original size: default `2`,
range `0.5`–`2`, inclusive. The default doubles portraits in both single- and
multi-repository playback; single-repository pixels therefore change too. Use
`--avatar-scale 1` for the original small-group disc diameter. Repository count
shrinks avatars only through the packing detail scale in [Playback](https://codestrand.pages.dev/playback/).
Name fonts retain their existing readability policy. `--gutter` independently controls
visible tile spacing (default `4` reference pixels at full detail, `0` allowed); the
outer margin is 24 pixels.
Visible avatars keep their names, including during travel and idle fade-out.
Crowded playback shrinks avatars and names; small groups retain their normal size.
Names first shrink to a minimum of 12 pixels at the reference 1280×720 viewport,
then try nearby free lane positions. Truncation is the last resort when the full name
cannot fit at the minimum size. Names prefer to avoid every repository’s content
rectangle and labels, with edge overlap permitted when no clear lane fits.
Name placement uses the default fitted view, including when preview is orbited or zoomed.
Playback time drives crowd scaling and placement, so export speed does not change them.

Preview and export stay offline by default: local overrides and cached portraits are
used, with the coloured sphere as the fallback. Add `--fetch-avatars` to either command
to opt in to network requests before playback starts. Export never fetches during frame
capture.

```sh
codestrand preview --repository /path/to/repo --fetch-avatars
codestrand export frames --repository /path/to/repo --fetch-avatars
```

Resolution stops at the first usable portrait, in the following order:

1. Explicit `avatar`: local file or cached/fetched HTTPS image. An unavailable local
   file warns and continues below. An unavailable HTTPS override keeps the default glyph
   (or its previous cached portrait), without account lookups.
2. Explicit `github`, then explicit `gitlab` using the GitLab.com Users API.
3. GitHub noreply login, then the commit author's GitHub account when a remote points
   to github.com (`origin` preferred). An explicit GitHub login replaces inferred
   GitHub lookup. The commit API runs at most once per distinct unresolved email per run.
4. GitLab.com email lookup, only with **both** `--fetch-avatars` and
   `--gitlab-email-avatars`.
5. Gravatar using `gravatar` when provided, otherwise the commit email, hashed with
   SHA-256 after trimming and lowercasing; `d=404` avoids Gravatar placeholders.
6. Default coloured sphere.

`GH_TOKEN` or `GITHUB_TOKEN`, when present, authenticates only GitHub API requests.
Public repositories work without a token; private repositories need a token with
repository access. GitLab lookups are unauthenticated and support GitLab.com only.
Rate limits and network failures leave playback available. HTTPS uses Rustls with ring
and the operating system trust store on Linux, macOS and Windows.

## Privacy and network settings

`--fetch-avatars` alone **never sends raw commit emails**. GitLab email lookup is off by
default, even when fetching is enabled. Opt in explicitly for each invocation:

```sh
codestrand export frames --repository /path/to/repo --fetch-avatars --gitlab-email-avatars
```

- No fetch flags: no requests; local overrides and cache only.
- `--fetch-avatars`, remote `avatar`: the override host receives the configured URL,
  including path and query.
- `--fetch-avatars`, GitHub: GitHub receives the configured or noreply login, or the
  repository and commit SHA. The image host receives the image URL, possibly containing
  a numeric account ID.
- `--fetch-avatars`, `gitlab`: GitLab.com receives the configured username. The returned
  image host receives the avatar URL.
- `--fetch-avatars`, Gravatar: Gravatar receives the normalized email's SHA-256 hash,
  never the email.
- Both flags, GitLab email: GitLab.com receives the trimmed, lowercased commit email
  in a URL query. The returned image host receives the avatar URL.

Identifiers and email hashes are identifying information. GitLab may return an external
avatar URL; fetching follows that URL unless the host is `gravatar.com` or a subdomain.
GitLab Gravatar URLs are treated as misses so the configured Gravatar step decides.
HTTPS redirects can also contact another image host.
An explicit avatar URL can itself contain identifying information supplied by the user.
GitHub credentials are never added to GitLab or image requests. Diagnostics show counts,
not emails or request URLs. Local avatar overrides do not require either fetch flag.

## Cache

Portraits and account resolutions live under `codestrand/avatars-v2/` in the platform
cache directory, keyed by a hash of email, explicit accounts, override, remote and GitLab
email setting. Remote overrides are keyed only by URL. Existing GitHub/Gravatar-only
cache entries remain usable. For account lookups, changing the GitLab email flag selects
a separate cache entry; pass `--gitlab-email-avatars` without
`--fetch-avatars` to reuse an opted-in portrait offline. The email flag alone never
enables network requests.
Portraits are resized to 128-pixel PNG files beside small JSON account records.
Fetching covers only contributors in the selected playback window, with a 30-second
total network budget. Entries refresh after seven days when fetching is enabled;
offline playback can reuse expired images. Failed refreshes retain cached images.
`--no-cache` disables avatar cache reads and writes too; local overrides still work.
Delete the directory to clear saved avatars. Circular portraits retain the contributor
colour as a ring; contributors without images keep the coloured sphere.

Cache reads and writes reject linked directories in every path component. An unusable
cache is treated as a miss; no linked destination is read or written.

---

Source: https://codestrand.pages.dev/security/

# Privacy and local processing

Codestrand makes no application network requests by default. Git import, planning
and rendering run locally; repositories are not uploaded. Avatar fetching is opt-in.

## Avatar requests

`--fetch-avatars` enables HTTPS requests for selected contributors. Depending on the
available portrait and account information, requests can disclose:

- A GitHub repository's owner and name and a commit hash to `api.github.com`, to find
  the matching account. API authentication uses `GH_TOKEN`, or `GITHUB_TOKEN` when
  `GH_TOKEN` is unset or not valid Unicode. An empty `GH_TOKEN` disables authentication
  without falling back to `GITHUB_TOKEN`; empty tokens are ignored. GitHub avatar
  servers receive the account name or numeric ID.
- A SHA-256 digest of a selected email address, or its configured Gravatar address,
  to Gravatar when a portrait is still missing. The address is trimmed and lowercased
  first. A hash is not anonymity:
  someone who knows an address can calculate the same value.
- A configured GitLab username to GitLab. Raw email lookup at GitLab requires both
  `--fetch-avatars` and `--gitlab-email-avatars`.
- A configured remote avatar URL to its HTTPS server, and any redirect destination.

Codestrand does not add source file paths, source contents or diff text to these
requests. Servers also receive ordinary connection information such as the source
IP address and the Codestrand user agent. Configured URLs can contain whatever
information their author put in them.

## What CI checks

- Only Codestrand depends on `ureq`, `rustls` is reached only through `ureq`, and
  neither `bevy_asset` nor `gix-transport` enables an HTTP feature.
- A Linux PNG export of a small local repository, with the history cache on, runs
  under `strace` in an empty network namespace and fails on any IP socket or Unix
  socket connection outside an allow-list.

The trace covers Linux and the code paths that export exercises. Preview, video
encoding, avatar fetching, macOS and Windows are not traced.

## Local files and processes

The history cache contains commit IDs and dates, contributor names and email
addresses, file paths, change counts and sampled source lines in plain text.
Portrait images and account lookup results are cached locally too. These files are
not encrypted by Codestrand. `--no-cache` disables reading and writing its caches.

The cache is under `codestrand` in the operating system's user cache directory:
`%LOCALAPPDATA%` on Windows, `~/Library/Caches` on macOS, and `$XDG_CACHE_HOME` or
`~/.cache` on Linux. History snapshots use per-repository subdirectories;
portrait data uses `avatars-v2`.

Video export starts FFmpeg and sends it rendered frames through standard input.
Codestrand's production import and renderer do not launch Git, repository hooks,
external diff drivers or other subprocesses.

Before planning, Codestrand compares a planning-memory estimate with available physical
memory. The estimate excludes the renderer and video encoder; it can be conservative
on some inputs and too low on others. It is not a process-memory limit or reservation.
Windowed planning bounds retained travel windows and checkpoints, not total process
memory. The available-memory snapshot excludes swap and container or job-specific limits.

This describes Codestrand's own behavior. It cannot promise what a user-selected
encoder executable does, or keep an operating system from accessing a network-mounted
repository, cache, avatar file or output path. HTTPS avatar requests use environment
proxy settings and the system certificate verifier. Operating-system services and other
software are outside this guarantee.

---

Source: https://codestrand.pages.dev/troubleshooting/

# Troubleshooting

## Command not found or missing options

Open a new terminal after installing and confirm the installation directory is on
`PATH`. Use `codestrand --version` and `codestrand --help` to check which binary
runs. The guides describe 0.2.0; upgrade an older release if an option is
missing. See [installation](https://codestrand.pages.dev/getting-started/installation/) for supported targets.

## Repository or revision cannot be read

Use a local repository path rather than a remote URL. Quote paths with spaces and
check the revision exists locally. Obtain a complete clone: shallow or partial
repositories can lack commits or objects needed for import. Inspect without
starting the renderer:

```sh
codestrand inspect /path/to/repository --revision HEAD
```

For stale or damaged playback cache data, retry with `--no-cache`. Inspection
always reads directly from Git. A later inclusive `--start-date` reads less history;
the first load of a large repository can take time.

## Graphics window or export fails

Both preview and export need a working graphics adapter. Preview also needs a
windowing environment. Update graphics drivers and try a local desktop session
for preview. `inspect` works without a GPU.
For slow source-checkout playback, use `cargo run --locked --release -- preview`.

## Source build fails

Install the Rust toolchain and native build prerequisites. Linux release builds
install ALSA, systemd/udev, X11, Xcursor, Xi, Xrandr, Wayland, EGL and xkbcommon
development packages. Wayland support requires `libwayland-dev` and `libxkbcommon-dev`
on Debian/Ubuntu, or `wayland-devel` and `libxkbcommon-devel` on Fedora.
Package names differ by distribution. Windows source builds need the
MSVC C++ build tools; macOS builds need the Xcode command-line tools.

## Export directory already exists

Choose a new directory for each export. Codestrand rejects an existing directory
rather than overwriting frames. Match FFmpeg's input framerate to the export's
`--fps`; see [export](https://codestrand.pages.dev/export/).

## Contributor configuration or portraits fail

An explicitly selected `--contributors` file must exist. Unknown TOML keys,
malformed TOML and duplicate emails are errors. A missing default file is allowed.
See the [configuration example](https://codestrand.pages.dev/contributors/).

Portraits stay offline unless `--fetch-avatars` is supplied. Network errors and
rate limits leave coloured spheres or previously cached images available.
`--no-cache` disables portrait reuse as well as history caching. Private GitHub
repositories need an API token with access.

## Report a problem

Terminal diagnostics escape control characters in paths and dependency error chains.
For example, an escape character is printed as `\u{1b}` rather than changing terminal
colour or interpreting a terminal command.

Include the version, operating system, exact command and error text in a
[GitHub issue](https://github.com/owenlamont/codestrand/issues). Remove private
repository paths, author identities and credentials before sharing logs or JSON.

---

Source: https://codestrand.pages.dev/ai-agents/

# Using Codestrand with AI agents

Coding agents can run Codestrand for you: inspect a repository, open a preview or export
frames and video. This page lists the context Codestrand publishes for them; the rest of
these docs cover the CLI itself.

## The Codestrand agent skill

The agent skill, `skills/codestrand/SKILL.md` in the
[repository](https://github.com/owenlamont/codestrand), teaches an agent the commands,
the export manifest, what leaves the machine and the common failures. Install it for
your user with the GitHub CLI:

```sh
gh skill install owenlamont/codestrand codestrand --agent claude-code --scope user
```

Swap `--agent` for `codex`, `cursor`, `github-copilot` or another host listed by
`gh skill install --help`. The skill installs from the latest release, so it is
available from the first release after 0.2.0. A test checks that every option the skill
names is in `--help` and that every command it shows parses.

## Prompting in AGENTS.md

A line in a repository's `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` points agents at the tool:

> Visualise this repository's history with `codestrand preview --repository .`, or
> export it with `codestrand export <new directory> --repository .`. Do not pass
> `--fetch-avatars` without asking: it sends contributor lookups to GitHub and Gravatar.

## Feeding the docs to an LLM

The docs site publishes [llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org) files for agents that read
documentation directly:

- [llms.txt](llms.txt): an index of every page with a one-line summary.
- [llms-full.txt](llms-full.txt): every page's Markdown in one file.

Both are generated from these pages by `scripts/gen_llms_txt.py`.

---

Source: https://codestrand.pages.dev/related-tools/

# Related tools

Codestrand is inspired by [Gource][gource]; other Git history visualisers and
Gource helpers offer several ways to explore a repository.

## Gource and helpers

| Tool | View or role | Built with | Runs as |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Gource][gource] | File trees and contributors | OpenGL | Desktop; frame output |
| [Rource (AdamLeyshon)][logs] | Multi-repo logs and aliases | Rust | CLI for Gource |
| [gourcers][gourcers] | Clone repos and merge logs | Rust | CLI for Gource |
| [Envisaged][envisaged] | Git history videos | Python, Gource, FFmpeg | CLI; web UI |
| [Envisaged Redux][redux] | Git history videos | Gource, FFmpeg | Docker; web preview |

## Gource-style trees

| Tool | View | Built with | Runs as |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Gource View][view] | Trees and contributors | Node.js server | Browser; MP4 export |
| [Rource (kauandotnet)][rource] | Animated trees | Rust, WASM | Desktop; browser |

## Cities, networks and treemaps

| Tool | View | Built with | Runs as |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Sourcity][sourcity] | Voxel cities and robots | .NET, Raylib-cs | Desktop |
| [Git City][city] | City and farm history replay | Electron | Desktop Git client |
| [Repo Visualizer][network] | Import networks | Canvas, WebGL | Browser; video |
| [strata][strata] | Treemaps, trees and charts | Rust, TypeScript/D3 | Browser; video |
| [gitatlas][atlas] | Animated file treemaps | Rust, FFmpeg | CLI video renderer |

[gource]: https://github.com/acaudwell/Gource
[logs]: https://github.com/AdamLeyshon/rource
[gourcers]: https://github.com/campbellcole/gourcers
[envisaged]: https://github.com/utensils/Envisaged
[redux]: https://envisaged-redux.vercel.app/
[view]: https://github.com/schlunsen/gource-view
[rource]: https://github.com/kauandotnet/rource
[sourcity]: https://github.com/mii-nipah/sourcity
[city]: https://github.com/maximalcode/git-city
[network]: https://github.com/Jany-M/repo-visualizer
[strata]: https://github.com/MrSeal04/strata
[atlas]: https://github.com/SupremeVoid/gitatlas
